title: The Receptor That Does Not Come Back

scenes.tts: How can a cell destroy a membrane-spanning receptor without leaving part of it behind? In chapter one, the receptor escaped. It released its L D L in acid and left before the end. But some receptors are meant to be destroyed.
scenes.narration: How can a cell destroy a membrane-spanning receptor without leaving part of it behind? In chapter one, the receptor escaped. It released its LDL in acid and left before the end. But some receptors are meant to be destroyed.
scenes.caption: How can a cell destroy a membrane-spanning receptor without leaving part of it behind? In chapter one, the receptor escaped. It released its LDL in acid and left before the end. But some receptors are meant to be destroyed.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD is chapter 1's, unchanged (fixed camera): a cross-section of one patch of cell edge filling the frame; a thick GREY plasma membrane across the top third, OUTSIDE above it in a dark navy wash, the CYTOSOL below in a warm dark-grey wash; one large round EARLY ENDOSOME mid-frame, left of centre (about 30% of frame height); a smaller round LYSOSOME with a RED outline lower right. Every lumen (endosome, lysosome, vesicle opening from the surface) is filled with the SAME navy wash as the outside. Chapter 1 colours keep their meaning: LDL receptor TEAL, LDL GOLD, acid a ROSE tint. New colours for this chapter: growth-factor receptor SKY BLUE (a bar crossing the membrane, same shape as the teal receptor), its signal molecule a small WHITE dot, ubiquitin tag a small LIME-GREEN chip on the receptor's tail, ESCRT a cluster of CORAL blocks, PCSK9 a CYAN wedge. Slow ambient motion throughout: gold LDL drifts outside, receptors jiggle in membranes. Open on the world already built. Immediately brighten a SKY-BLUE receptor spanning the endosome membrane; a white dashed arrow runs from it to the red lysosome, with a question mark at the arrow's head. Text across the top, white, size 34: 'Destroy the receptor itself. How?' On 'chapter one', faintly trace chapter 1's TEAL loop and GOLD one-way arrow over the world (opacity 40%). A teal receptor rides a thin tubule up and out of the endosome and back to the surface (a 3 s replay; tag 'chapter 1', white, size 28, bottom right). On 'meant to be destroyed', the teal loop fades and the sky-blue receptor and dashed route brighten again.
Title 'The Receptor That Does Not Come Back' fades in over the top band for 2 s while the question text fades out. The dashed arrow and question mark stay. Gold LDL keeps drifting outside.

scenes.tts: Many activated growth-factor receptors are like this, shown here in sky blue. Activation can add ubiquitin, a small protein shown in green. The tagged receptors enter an early endosome. Ubiquitin helps mark them for lysosomal degradation.
scenes.narration: Many activated growth-factor receptors are like this, shown here in sky blue. Activation can add ubiquitin, a small protein shown in green. The tagged receptors enter an early endosome. Ubiquitin helps mark them for lysosomal degradation.
scenes.caption: Many activated growth-factor receptors are like this, shown here in sky blue. Activation can add ubiquitin, a small protein shown in green. The tagged receptors enter an early endosome. Ubiquitin helps mark them for lysosomal degradation.
scenes.visual: At the top membrane, a white signal dot docks on a sky-blue receptor (small snap, white flash). On 'ubiquitin', a lime-green chip clicks onto the receptor's cytosolic tail. Label 'ubiquitin tag' in lime green, size 30, beside the chip. The pair rides a small schematic endocytic vesicle down into the endosome (2 s), and the sky-blue receptor settles in the endosome membrane, its outer end facing the navy lumen and its tagged tail in the warm cytosol. Two more tagged sky-blue receptors are already there. Label 'growth-factor receptor' in sky blue, size 30, beside the endosome.

scenes.tts: Here is the problem. The receptor sits in the endosome's own membrane, with its tail out in the cytosol. Suppose this endosome simply fused with a lysosome. Could the enzymes inside reach the whole receptor?
scenes.narration: Here is the problem. The receptor sits in the endosome's own membrane, with its tail out in the cytosol. Suppose this endosome simply fused with a lysosome. Could the enzymes inside reach the whole receptor?
scenes.caption: Here is the problem. The receptor sits in the endosome's own membrane, with its tail out in the cytosol. Suppose this endosome simply fused with a lysosome. Could the enzymes inside reach the whole receptor?
scenes.visual: Slow push-in (scale 1.4x) on one sky-blue receptor in the endosome's outer membrane. Its outer end glows on the navy (lumen) side; its tail with the green chip glows on the warm-grey (cytosol) side. A schematic replay shows the endosome sliding to the red lysosome and their outlines merging (tag 'schematic, suppose', white, size 28). Small RED scissor-shaped enzyme blocks appear in the merged lumen and drift toward the receptor. On 'Could the enzymes', the rest of the world dims to 50% and a question card appears at the top, white, size 36: 'Can enzymes reach every part?'
Thinking pause: hold the question card. Only slow ambient motion: the red enzyme blocks drift in the lumen without touching anything, the endosome outline breathes slightly. Nothing is revealed.

scenes.tts: Not all of it. The enzymes work in the lumen, so only the part facing the lumen is within their reach. The cell gets around this by moving the receptor off that outer membrane.
scenes.narration: Not all of it. The enzymes work in the lumen, so only the part facing the lumen is within their reach. The cell gets around this by moving the receptor off that outer membrane.
scenes.caption: Not all of it. The enzymes work in the lumen, so only the part facing the lumen is within their reach. The cell gets around this by moving the receptor off that outer membrane.
scenes.visual: The question card fades; the world returns to full brightness and the merged outline separates again into the endosome and the lysosome (undo the schematic replay). On 'only the part facing the lumen', the receptor's lumen-facing end is outlined in red as within reach, while its tail and green chip on the cytosol side stay unoutlined and a label 'out of reach' appears beside the tail (white, size 28). On 'moving the receptor', a white arrow points from the receptor into the middle of the endosome lumen. Push back out to the full world.
Rest beat: the white arrow into the lumen holds; the sky-blue receptor in the rim jiggles; red enzyme blocks wait in the lysosome; gold LDL drifts outside.

scenes.tts: From the early endosome on, patches of its outer membrane, the limiting membrane, bud inward into the lumen. Each bud pinches off as a small vesicle inside. An endosome full of them is a multivesicular body.
scenes.narration: From the early endosome on, patches of its outer membrane, the limiting membrane, bud inward into the lumen. Each bud pinches off as a small vesicle inside. An endosome full of them is a multivesicular body.
scenes.caption: From the early endosome on, patches of its outer membrane, the limiting membrane, bud inward into the lumen. Each bud pinches off as a small vesicle inside. An endosome full of them is a multivesicular body.
scenes.visual: Three small patches of the endosome's membrane dimple inward, away from the cytosol, deepen into buds, and pinch off as small round inner vesicles that float in the navy lumen. The inside of each inner vesicle is the warm-grey CYTOSOL wash (it was cytosol when the bud closed; do not narrate this). Label 'limiting membrane' in white, size 28, on the endosome rim. Then four more inner vesicles form while the label morphs to 'multivesicular body' (white, size 30) above the endosome. Some inner vesicles carry sky-blue receptors in their membrane; draw them only after the next scene's sorting cue if timing allows.

scenes.tts: What decides which proteins go into the buds? Complexes called E S C R T, in coral, recognize the ubiquitin tag. They sort the tagged receptors into the inner vesicles. In this comparison, an untagged protein stays behind.
scenes.narration: What decides which proteins go into the buds? Complexes called ESCRT, in coral, recognize the ubiquitin tag. They sort the tagged receptors into the inner vesicles. In this comparison, an untagged protein stays behind.
scenes.caption: What decides which proteins go into the buds? Complexes called ESCRT, in coral, recognize the ubiquitin tag. They sort the tagged receptors into the inner vesicles. In this comparison, an untagged protein stays behind.
scenes.visual: Coral blocks gather on the cytosolic face of the endosome membrane and grab the green chips on the sky-blue receptor tails. Each coral cluster pulls its tagged receptor into a membrane patch, the patch buds into the lumen and pinches off, carrying the receptor inside the new inner vesicle. One untagged protein in the limiting membrane (a plain GREY bar with no chip) is passed over by the coral blocks and stays in the rim; small label 'untagged' (white, size 28) beside it. Label 'ESCRT' in coral, size 30, beside the first cluster. As each bud closes, its coral blocks let go and return to the cytosol.

Rest beat: the multivesicular body with its inner vesicles (some carrying sky-blue receptors) drifts slowly toward the lysosome; coral blocks drift back into the cytosol; the untagged grey protein stays in the rim.

scenes.tts: The multivesicular body then fuses with a lysosome. Each inner vesicle now floats whole in the lumen, receptor and all, and the enzymes digest it. This is how those receptors are switched off.
scenes.narration: The multivesicular body then fuses with a lysosome. Each inner vesicle now floats whole in the lumen, receptor and all, and the enzymes digest it. This is how those receptors are switched off.
scenes.caption: The multivesicular body then fuses with a lysosome. Each inner vesicle now floats whole in the lumen, receptor and all, and the enzymes digest it. This is how those receptors are switched off.
scenes.visual: The multivesicular body drifts to the red lysosome at lower right and fuses with it (outlines merge). The red enzyme blocks swarm the inner vesicles; each inner vesicle with its sky-blue receptor breaks into small sky-blue and membrane fragments that spread through the lumen. Do not depict the fate of the green ubiquitin tag. The whole merged compartment pulses red once. Label 'digested' in sky blue, size 30. On 'switched off', a small white signal pulse associated with the receptor being digested fades out; leave any receptors and signal dots at the surface unchanged (tag 'schematic', white, size 28).
Rest beat: sky-blue and green fragments spread slowly through the lysosome lumen and fade; gold LDL drifts outside.

scenes.tts: So the endosome sorts more than cargo. A receptor left in the limiting membrane can still return. A ubiquitin tag can select a receptor for inward budding. The lysosome can then digest all of it.
scenes.narration: So the endosome sorts more than cargo. A receptor left in the limiting membrane can still return. A ubiquitin tag can select a receptor for inward budding. The lysosome can then digest all of it.
scenes.caption: So the endosome sorts more than cargo. A receptor left in the limiting membrane can still return. A ubiquitin tag can select a receptor for inward budding. The lysosome can then digest all of it.
scenes.visual: Over the world, chapter 1's TEAL loop reappears (membrane, endosome, tubule, back to membrane) with a small label 'return' in teal, size 30. Beside it a SKY-BLUE path traces from the endosome membrane inward into an inner vesicle and on to the lysosome. A small green chip rides only to the inward-budding step; the sky-blue receptor path continues to the lysosome, without specifying the tag's fate. Add a label 'tagged: inward, then digested' in sky blue, size 30. The endosome pulses rose and a white ring marks it as the place where the two paths split. Both paths stay on screen.
Rest beat: a teal dot runs once around the teal loop while a sky-blue dot with a green chip runs the inward path and stops in the lysosome. Ambient drift continues.

scenes.tts: Even a looping receptor can be pulled out of its loop. P C S K 9, in cyan, is a protein that cells secrete. It binds one small part of the L D L receptor's outer region.
scenes.narration: Even a looping receptor can be pulled out of its loop. PCSK9, in cyan, is a protein that cells secrete. It binds one small part of the LDL receptor's outer region.
scenes.caption: Even a looping receptor can be pulled out of its loop. PCSK9, in cyan, is a protein that cells secrete. It binds one small part of the LDL receptor's outer region.
scenes.visual: The sky-blue path fades. An empty teal LDL receptor stands in the top membrane. A cyan wedge drifts in from the outside wash and docks on a small segment of the teal receptor's outer part (label the docking segment 'one small part', white, size 28; no structure, just a block). Label 'PCSK9' in cyan, size 30. Both enter in a small schematic endocytic vesicle.

scenes.tts: Cultured human cells show what happens next. A receptor bound this way goes to the lysosome instead of returning to the surface. Its loop has become a one-way trip. The receptor does not come back to grip again.
scenes.narration: Cultured human cells show what happens next. A receptor bound this way goes to the lysosome instead of returning to the surface. Its loop has become a one-way trip. The receptor does not come back to grip again.
scenes.caption: Cultured human cells show what happens next. A receptor bound this way goes to the lysosome instead of returning to the surface. Its loop has become a one-way trip. The receptor does not come back to grip again.
scenes.visual: Inside the endosome, the teal receptor with its cyan wedge does NOT enter the recycling tubule: the tubule grows and pinches off empty. Trace a schematic teal route from the endosome toward the red lysosome, but hide the intervening sorting steps behind a short dotted segment labelled 'sorting not shown' (white, size 28). At the lysosome, show the endpoint label 'LDL receptor degraded' in teal, size 30; do not draw the membrane-spanning receptor fragmenting in the lysosome lumen. On 'one-way trip', the teal loop over the world breaks open and its end bends into a one-way arrow to the lysosome, matching the gold arrow. Tag 'in cultured human cells tested' bottom right, white, size 28.
Rest beat: the broken teal loop and the gold arrow both point into the lysosome; teal and gold fragments drift in it; a new gold LDL drifts past an empty patch of surface membrane.

scenes.tts: So a cell can destroy a receptor, not just its cargo. A ubiquitin tag can select the receptor for inward budding at the endosome. Inward budding puts the whole receptor within lysosomal enzymes' reach.
scenes.narration: So a cell can destroy a receptor, not just its cargo. A ubiquitin tag can select the receptor for inward budding at the endosome. Inward budding puts the whole receptor within lysosomal enzymes' reach.
scenes.caption: So a cell can destroy a receptor, not just its cargo. A ubiquitin tag can select the receptor for inward budding at the endosome. Inward budding puts the whole receptor within lysosomal enzymes' reach.
scenes.visual: Camera holds on the full world. A sky-blue receptor in the endosome membrane gets a green chip, and a coral cluster selects it for an inner bud. Once the bud closes, stop following the tag; the multivesicular body fuses with the lysosome, where the inner vesicle and receptor break into fragments. Meanwhile, a teal receptor rides a tubule back to the surface. The two paths from the rule scene glow once, teal and sky blue.

End card over the dimmed world: 'Inward budding puts the whole receptor within lysosomal enzymes’ reach.' in white, size 40, with 'whole receptor' in sky blue and 'Inward budding' in coral. Small 'biochemistrypedia.com' beneath.
